name: Rania Haddad
headline: 28, part-time university tutor and freelance translator, Amman
title: The Dinner Invitation
situation: Rania's friend Layla, a fellow adjunct from the English department, invites her to a small family dinner this Friday. "Please, don't bring anything," Layla says on the phone. "I know you're busy, and you have enough to carry. Just come and spend time." Rania knows that in Jordanian custom, showing up empty-handed to a meal feels rude, even though Layla is also Jordanian and knows the custom herself. Rania has a jar of apricot jam she made and a fresh loaf of bread at home. She could bring them anyway, explaining it's a small token of appreciation, or she could respect Layla's request and arrive without anything, trusting that her presence is enough.

context.relationship_profiles:
Layla is one of the few colleagues who knows Rania's per-course situation and has never pressed her about money; she often invites Rania to family meals at her home.
At department gatherings, Layla sits beside Rania and quietly adds extra food to her plate, and Rania has never commented on it.
Layla's mother treats Rania like a daughter, calls her 'Auntie' in jest, and always sends her home with leftovers.
context.tendencies:
At every prior invitation to Layla's house, Rania has brought bread, jam, or a small jar of olives even when told not to.
When a colleague offers her a ride or a meal, she usually deflects the kindness but later leaves behind something small—a copied handout, a translated passage, a teacake.
She keeps a mental ledger of every kindness and answers it with a tangible gift, sometimes to the confusion of the giver.
context.current_state:
Rania has been up late translating a lease agreement for two nights and is running on less sleep than usual.
This morning she baked a fresh loaf and sealed a new batch of apricot jam, and the kitchen still smells of warm bread.
She is looking forward to a quiet evening after a heavy week of marking, though she also knows her pantry is nearly empty.
context.immediate_memories:
Layla's phrase 'don't bring anything' reminds Rania of last spring, when she brought a loaf anyway and Layla's mother exclaimed that it was better than the bakery's.
The sight of the jam jar on the counter recalls the summer she and Layla made jam together after Layla's father's funeral, working side by side in silence.
context.reflective_memories:
Rania remembers her grandmother's rule that a visitor should never arrive with empty hands, and that even a single piece of bread counted as respect.
She also remembers how, after her divorce, her brother's family took her in without asking, and how small offerings—tea, envelopes, a scarf—helped her feel less like a dependent.
She has noticed that Layla never keeps score, which sometimes makes it harder for Rania to simply accept a generous invitation.
